charlesWesley.title: Charles Wesley
charlesWesley.subtitle: December 18, 1707 — March 29, 1788 · Epworth → London
charlesWesley.bio: Co-founder of Methodism with his brother John, Charles Wesley is above all the greatest hymnographer in the English language. Its 6,500 hymns have shaped global Protestant spirituality and remain sung in all Christian traditions in the 21st century.

hymns.title: And Can It Be (1738)
hymns.fr: What a marvel — can I believe it?
hymns.occasion: Composed shortly after Charles's conversion, on May 21, 1738, 3 days before John's Aldersgate experience.
hymns.stanza:
And can it be that I should gain
An interest in the Saviour's blood?
Died He for me, who caused His pain?
For me, who Him to death pursued?
Amazing love! how can it be
That Thou, my God, should not die for me?
hymns.fr_stanza:
What a marvel! Can I have part
To the blood shed by my Savior?
Was it for me that he suffered,
For me, the cause of his pain?
Amazing love! How can it be
That you, my God, died for me?
hymns.theme: Justification by faith, wonder of grace

hymns.title: O for a Thousand Tongues (1739)
hymns.occasion: Written for the first anniversary of his conversion. It is the first hymn in the first official Methodist collection.
hymns.stanza:
O for a thousand tongues to sing
My great Redeemer's praise,
The glories of my God and King,
The triumphs of His grace!
hymns.fr_stanza:
O for a thousand tongues to sing
The praises of my Redeemer,
The glories of my God-King,
The triumphs of His grace!

hymns.title: Hark! The Herald Angels Sing (1739)
hymns.fr: Here is the angel of the Lord
hymns.occasion: Originally 'Hark how all the welkin rings' — title modified by George Whitefield. One of the most sung Christmas carols in the world.
hymns.stanza:
Hark! the herald angels sing,
'Glory to the newborn King!
Peace on earth and mercy mild,
God and sinners reconciled!'
hymns.fr_stanza:
Here is the angel of the Lord!
Glory to the newborn King!
Peace on earth, immense grace,
God and sinners reconciled!

hymns.title: Christ the Lord Is Risen Today (1739)
hymns.occasion: Written for the First Methodist Chapel (The Foundery, London). Sung on Easter morning around the world.
hymns.stanza:
Christ the Lord is risen today, Alleluia!
Sons of men and angels say, Alleluia!
Raise your joys and triumphs high, Alleluia!
Sing, ye heavens, and earth reply, Alleluia!
hymns.fr_stanza:
Christ the Lord is risen, Hallelujah!
Angels and men, proclaim, Alleluia!
Raise your joys and your songs, Alleluia!
May the heavens and the earth respond, Alleluia!
hymns.theme: Resurrection, victory over death, Easter joy

hymns.title: Love Divine, All Loves Excelling (1747)
hymns.fr: Divine love, which surpasses all love
hymns.occasion: Canticle on Sanctification — Charles's theological masterpiece. Expresses the 'Christian perfection' dear to John Wesley.
hymns.stanza:
Love divine, all loves excelling,
Joy of heaven to earth come down!
Fix in us Thy humble dwelling,
All Thy faithful thanks crown.
hymns.fr_stanza:
Divine love, surpassing all love,
Joy from heaven descended to earth!
Come and stay in our humble abode,
Crown all your faithful mercies.
hymns.theme: Sanctification, Christian perfection, love of God

hymns.title: Soldiers of Christ, Arise (1749)
hymns.occasion: Written during the period of persecution against Methodists. Encourage believers to put on the spiritual armor of Ephesians 6.
hymns.stanza:
Soldiers of Christ, arise,
And put your armor on,
Strong in the strength which God supplies
Through His eternal Son.
hymns.fr_stanza:
Soldiers of Christ, arise,
Put on your armor,
Strong in the strength that God grants
By his eternal Son.
hymns.theme: Spiritual warfare, perseverance, armor from Ephesians 6

biography.text: Charles Wesley was born on December 18, 1707 in Epworth, 18th of 19 children of Samuel and Susanna. Born prematurely, he is so weak that he does not cry and remains wrapped in wool for several weeks. His mother Susanna devotes special attention to him. As a child, he showed early musical and literary sensitivity under his mother's rigorous education.

Charles attended Westminster School (1716) where he excelled in Greek and Latin. In 1726 he entered Christ Church College, Oxford. It was he who, in 1729, founded the 'Holy Club' in Oxford - before his brother John took over its management. George Whitefield will join them. Charles was ordained as an Anglican deacon and priest in 1735, just before the mission to Georgia.

Charles's conversion precedes John's by 3 days. On May 21, 1738, sick and lying at a friend's house, Charles read Isaiah 40 and the words struck him like a revelation. He receives assurance of his salvation. That evening he wrote 'And Can It Be' — his first great hymn. When John tells him of his own conversion 3 days later, they sing together.

For 50 years, Charles transformed Wesleyan theology into song. He composes on average one hymn per week — sometimes several per day. He composed on horseback, dictating the verses to his companion. His hymns are his preaching: they teach grace, sanctification, the Trinity, resurrection with incomparable lyrical beauty. John said that Charles' hymns were his best theology.
